claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn is initially a single-phase FCC alloy.
The initial crystal is defect-free or has a low vacancy concentration.
Dislocation nucleation at yielding is primarily thermally activated emission from pre-existing vacancy clusters or solute-rich regions rather than homogeneous nucleation.
The emitted defects are Shockley partial dislocations with Burgers vectors of the 1/6<112> type.
Shockley partial emission creates intrinsic stacking faults on {111} planes.
At high strain rates, insufficient time for dislocation annihilation increases the dislocation density.
Yield strength is relatively insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength decreases monotonically as temperature increases from 77 K to 300 K.
Crystal orientation significantly influences the yield stress.
<11-1>-oriented crystals have a higher maximum yield stress than <110>-oriented crystals.
The <11-1> orientation has more favorable Schmid factors for partial-dislocation glide on {111} planes, whereas <110> has less favorable slip geometry.
The orientation-dependent Schmid factors determine the applied stress needed to reach the critical resolved shear stress.
The maximum yield stress for the <11-1> orientation will be 10–20% greater than that for the <110> orientation.
The observed HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults rather than a true FCC-to-HCP phase transformation.
An FCC-to-HCP transformation is kinetically suppressed under the specified simulation conditions.
The baseline simulations exhibit neither deformation twinning nor a phase transformation.
HRTEM combined with SAED can identify a characteristic 1/3{111} stacking-fault vector.
Distinct HCP diffraction peaks and long-range HCP periodicity would indicate a true HCP phase transformation.
Reversible annihilation of the HCP-like regions during heating without hysteresis would support their identification as stacking faults.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to polycrystalline or multiphase alloys, strain rates above 10^10 s^-1, or temperatures above 500 K.

contradictions.description: The initial state permits a defect-free crystal, while the proposed primary nucleation mechanism requires pre-existing vacancy clusters. The solute-rich-region alternative does not fully resolve the inconsistency for the asserted vacancy-cluster mechanism.

The hypothesis attributes the higher applied yield stress of <11-1> to a more favorable Schmid factor. Within a Schmid-factor mechanism, a more favorable slip orientation normally reaches a given critical resolved shear stress at a lower applied stress, so the stated causal direction is internally questionable.
